text: There are n planets and m one-way teleporters. Two planets are in the same kingdom if you can travel from each to the other. Print the number of kingdoms, and for each planet which kingdom it belongs to.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — a kingdom is a strongly connected component: a maximal set of planets where every planet can reach every other, following the teleporters' directions. Is that right?

Let me run through a small example. Say one to two to three and back to one, plus three to four and four to five. The triangle one, two, three is mutually reachable, so it's one kingdom. But four can't get back to three, and five can't get back to four — so four and five are each their own kingdom. Three kingdoms total.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to test mutual reachability for every pair — a BFS from each planet is n times n plus m. With n up to ten to the fifth, that's far too slow. This problem reminds me of Kosaraju's algorithm — strongly connected components in two linear DFS passes. The first pass on the original graph records a finish order. Then I process nodes in reverse finish order on the reversed graph; each DFS tree there is exactly one component.

Here's the plan. One: DFS the original graph, pushing a node to order after all its descendants finish. Two: reverse order, so the latest-finished node comes first. Three: DFS the reversed graph in that order, one label per component. One thing worth flagging — why the reversed graph is essential. The latest-finished node sits in a source component. On the original graph a source can reach several components downstream, so one DFS would merge them. Reversing every edge turns that source into a sink — from it you can only reach its own component, so one DFS traps exactly one. Also, the order matters for correctness, not just speed. Reverse finish order guarantees I always start from the current graph's source; peel it off, and the next unlabeled node is the next source. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. dfs1 walks the original graph and pushes a planet onto order only after all its descendants finish. dfs2 walks the reversed graph and stamps every planet it reaches with kingdom k. Main reads the teleporters, runs pass one from every unvisited planet, reverses order, then starts pass two from each unlabeled planet with a fresh k. That matches the plan. One thing worth flagging — I build rg in the same loop as g, so the reversed graph costs nothing extra. And comp of u being nonzero doubles as visited in the second pass, which is why kingdoms are numbered from one.

Let's dry-run the example. Pass one from planet one finishes them in the order five, four, three, two, one; reversed, that's one through five. The row that matters is the first: planet one is the latest to finish, so it's in a source component. On the reversed graph, its reachable set is trapped inside one, two, three — it can't leak into four or five. Then four and five each find only labeled neighbors, so they become kingdoms two and three. Output: three, then one, one, one, two, three. Corner cases: a single planet with no teleporters is one kingdom. A graph that's already one big cycle is one kingdom. A DAG makes every planet its own kingdom, so k equals n.

The time complexity is n plus m — two linear DFS passes. The space complexity is n plus m, for the two adjacency lists plus the arrays. In the worst case a long chain gives recursion depth n, so at ten to the fifth I'd bump the stack or go iterative. Oh, one more thing — Kosaraju needs the reverse graph and two passes; Tarjan's algorithm does it in one pass with dfn, low, and a stack. I chose Kosaraju because it's easier to explain and hard to get wrong.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You named the problem as strongly connected components immediately. You explained why the second pass must run on the reversed graph — the source-becomes-sink argument — not just that it does. And you were clear that reverse finish order is a correctness requirement. Good work.
